A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same universal, non-invasive mesh attack on BEV detectors, renamed from Meeseeks Mesh to SABER. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original nuScenes attack experiments, shape and placement ablations, and cross-model transfer and distance-robustness results in its appendices.

after.justification: v3 reports original digital attack experiments, expanded ablations and robustness evaluations, and physical experiments with fabricated adversarial objects.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces v1's minimum-distance occlusion check with a combined image-overlap and BEV convex-hull visibility test. Section 11 also introduces a physical-deployment variant using texture-only optimization, an additional lighting-perturbed training stage and masked total-variation regularization. These substantially extend the retained placement and three-loss optimization framework.

E1.justification: Both versions use nuScenes, but v3 adds captured physical scenes containing fabricated adversarial objects and nearby vehicles, including different viewpoints and partial occlusions (Sections 4.5 and 11). This extends evaluation from digitally inserted meshes to actual physical inputs.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates Adv3D as its competing attack method. v3 retains Adv3D and adds an explicit UAP comparison in Table 3, covering an invasive patch attack already cited in v1. This is a limited expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported loss weights alpha and beta change from 1 to 10, and Table 1 drops the ASR threshold of 0.2. New protocols include sequential six-view physical capture, 10-plus-5-epoch physical adaptation, GeoBEV evaluation, and testing BEVDet fine-tuned for two epochs with PGD examples replacing 10% of training data. The nuScenes split remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds loss-component and geometry-versus-color ablations (Tables 7–8), digital validation of the physical adaptation (Table 11), target-to-ego distance analysis (Table 13), defense robustness testing (Table 15), and physical cross-view and occlusion case studies (Figure 9). Earlier shape, random-placement and mesh-to-target distance analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experimental results. The additional experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Many matched white-box, shape, distance and transfer results are revised. For example, Table 1's BEVDet4D ASR0.3 without Real Occ changes from 0.321 to 0.530 while its NDS/mAP entries remain unchanged. v3 adds UAP, ablation, physical, GeoBEV and defense results; Table 2 replaces pedestrian/barrier AP entries with bicycle AP. Given the method and setting revisions, these are not uniformly comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: v3 adds mathematical definitions for the BEV visibility cone and combined occlusion criterion, replacing the scalar depth comparison, and defines masked, normalized total-variation regularization in Equation 10. These are limited formal extensions; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v1's central claim concerns the existence and effectiveness of spatially consistent universal attacks. v3 adds a central explanatory claim that these attacks expose over-reliance on contextual object-co-occurrence priors and significant dataset deficiencies, prominently stated in the abstract and introduction. Its conclusion also explicitly claims validation through physical experiments.

C2.justification: v3 expands contextual-prior and dataset-bias explanations and adds a physical-to-digital limitation attributed to RGB/CMYK printing differences. It removes v1's explicit limitations concerning BEVDet4D and random placement. The unchanged random-placement results, v1 Table 5 and v3 Table 6, are now presented as robustness evidence with a deployment-cost tradeoff.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies model-specific training times, 48GB GPU memory, 15 meshes at test time and a 7–27-meter random-placement range. It documents physical camera acquisition and calibration, lighting parameters, adaptation stages and PGD settings, and adds a project-page pointer. These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information; the newly stated test counts and placement range do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

R1.justification: The same three related-work themes and central distinction from Adv3D remain. v3 adds supporting references for newer BEV models, physical acquisition, rendering and defense methods, including GeoBEV, VGGT and PGD, while removing BEVFusion and BEV-DG citations. It also elaborates its positioning relative to invasive UAP attacks.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and results discussion are extensively rewritten, with an explicit contribution list and new SABER terminology. Implementation and shape details move into a reorganized supplement containing Sections 7–15, replacing the earlier Appendix A–C organization. These changes substantially alter the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the pipeline diagram, merges and rearranges v1 Figures 4 and 6 into Figure 4, and adds physical-experiment, acquisition and occlusion illustrations. Tables gain clean-baseline and percentage-drop columns alongside new experimental tables. Earlier appendix visualizations are retained as Figures 10–11.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1's feasibility and component evidence through documented physical demonstrations, loss/geometry ablations and defense testing. The revised occlusion reasoning and expanded implementation details further strengthen the work. These substantial gains are tempered by qualitative-only physical validation, stronger causal claims and removal of earlier robustness caveats. A new reporting error also remains: Table 2 claims a 55.6% mAP drop, whereas its displayed initial and adversarial values imply about 50.6%.
